newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: PM Sharif keeps Pakistan in suspense over cabinet.
newsitem.headline: PM Sharif keeps Pakistan in suspense over cabinet.

text.p: More than three weeks after his sweeping election victory, Pakistan's new Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif has yet to name a cabinet to run his troubled country.
During a tea break at an oil and gas conference in Islamabad on Tuesday, Sartaj Aziz, tipped to become finance minister, was asked when the cabinet would be formed. He smiled and walked on.
The same question put to an aide to President Farooq Leghari's elicited only "very soon, very soon", but no date.

The long delay has paralysed government business and provoked speculation about power struggles within Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML) as party heavyweights jostle for slots in the slimmed-down ministerial team he has promised.

"This sort of thing happens when you've got a top-heavy government with so many people aspiring to become ministers," said Awais Bangash, spokesman for the opposition Pakistan People's Party (PPP) led by former prime minister Benazir Bhutto.
He recalled that Bhutto was sworn in with four key cabinet ministers when she took power in October 1993. Sharif took his oath of office on February 16, but no ministers have been named.
"Sharif is a weak person who has a tendency to succumb to pressures from various groups," Bangash said.
Mohammad Ziauddin of the Karachi-based Dawn daily newspaper said Sharif, who has pledged to keep the cabinet small in line with an austerity drive, wanted to include fresh, young faces.
But he was finding it hard to balance this objective with the demands of his senior party colleagues, Ziauddin said.

Another problem, he argued, was the Council for Defence and National Security (CDNS), created last month by President Farooq Leghari as an advisory forum grouping top generals and the ministers of foreign affairs, finance, defence and interior.
"The CDNS is being considered a supra-cabinet and all Sharif's senior colleagues want to sit there," he said.

Most of Sharif's close colleagues are from his home province of Punjab. Including them in the CDNS would give it a "totally Punjabi profile", given that President Farooq Leghari and Chief of Army Staff General Jehangir Karamat are also Punjabis.
Pakistan's smaller provinces of Sindhi, North West Frontier Province and Balochistan have in the past resented what they see as the dominance of wealthy and populous Punjab.

Sharif may not have appointed his team, but he has made one impassioned speech to the nation in which he contrasted the high expectations of voters who gave the PML a thumping majority in parliament with the monumental tasks facing his government.
"You have given me a revolutionary mandate to pull the country out of the present crisis," he said on Sunday. "And I will, God willing, work with an equally revolutionary spirit."
Newspaper commentators have generally praised his speech, but have urged Sharif to end the current uncertainty.
"The sense of movement that was created by the address was slightly clouded by the fact that it had come in the absence of a cabinet," wrote Ghazi Salahuddin in The News daily.
Sharif's speech appeared to pre-empt many decisions that might normally be subject to cabinet scrutiny.
He launched a grand scheme to pay off the country's $30 billion national debt by asking expatriate Pakistanis to send their money home and pledged to cut wasteful public spending.

At the micro-level, he banned smoking in government offices, forbade lavish weddings, ordered the death penalty for gang-rapists, changed the weekly holiday to Sunday from Friday, promised to promote Islamic banking and opened a hotline for citizens to advise him how to make government more accountable.
